strengths: Spaced repetition consistently improves accuracy across all 5 benchmarks and 2 models, demonstrating robust gains.
The paper provides an ablation study for three components of the algorithm, and it seems that all 3 improve performance
The paper spends time clearly outlining their precise algorithm
The paper is well-written and clearly presented;

The paper tackled the important problem of data mixture & curriculum learning of instruction tuning for large language model and proposed a novel method, "space scheduling", quantitive results on 4 benchmark suite show the effectiveness of the proposed methods versus baseline or random mixture methods;
Detailed ablation and qualitative examples w.r.t other scheduling variants have been presented to show the effectiveness of the proposed
It is great to show the proposed methods are based on LoRA, which offers extra accessibility to large research community;
The introduction seems interesting. The analogy drawn to human learning processes is quite inspiring.
The author performed an ablation study to show the benefit of each main component of the proposed algorithm.
Motivating the technique with relevant psychology literature.
Applying the technique to instruction tuning LLMs, which is a research topic that is attracting considerable attention.
Conducting an ablation analysis on the components of the proposed algorithm.
weaknesses: The related work and contextualization of the current paper make it seem that this problem has not been studied before, which can be misleading. Better contextualizing the work in terms of prior research in this area will help highlight the novel contributions by this paper.

Though the results provide an ablation study, it is unclear where prior work lies in this spectrum. I would appreciate seeing a reasonable baseline to confirm that this work pushes along various fine‑tuning tradeoffs.
The paper should compare against simple baselines such as filtering sentences with extreme perplexity and against active learning methods like Data diets.

The algorithm should induce extra time overhead since examples have to be scored, and "currently difficult" examples may have to go through the model multiple times. The authors should report the time taken by both algorithms to evaluate this slowdown so one can evaluate whether this accuracy improvement is worth the additional cost.
It is not clear how connected the algorithm is to spaced repetition learning for humans; the connection to the psychological motivation is unclear.

Missing comparison in Table 1 versus Tulu as mentioned in 4.2 for the effectiveness of MERCURY versus original Tulu paper; also MT‑Bench or other human‑involved evaluations would be good to show comprehensive effectiveness.
Benefits seem enlarged for Math/Code with both MERCURY / Space Scheduling; the effect of adding OpenOrca dataset only should be ablated.
The scalability of the proposed method is questionable.
Some parts of the writing are ambiguous; a representative concept figure would be helpful.
Experimental results are not very strong; claiming overall performance improvement is risky because gain was only in four out of seven evaluations.
Impact of hyperparameter variations (e.g., $s_t$ and $\rho_0$) has not been analyzed; ablation studies on hyperparameters are necessary.
Explanations are missing for certain formulas, e.g., why the minimum score threshold is $z_t \leftarrow z_{max} - \kappa -1$.
Discussion of related work is lacking; spaced scheduling for deep learning has been considered in Hadi Amiri et al.
The proposed method does not appear to be motivated with a memory model; compare Amiri et al. or other works that motivate proposals based on a memory model.
Empirical part should include a comparison to another spaced scheduling method (e.g., Amiri et al.).

It is hard to conclude whether to use the proposed method or other online scheduling approaches; comparison to prior work on automated curriculum learning (e.g., Kreutzer et al.) would strengthen the empirical part.
